title: Fridge and freezer habits that save energy
description: Your fridge runs all day, every day, so small habits around temperature, seals and loading add up.

body.heading: Set temperatures that protect food, not icebergs
paragraphs: A fridge kept around 3 to 5 degrees Celsius keeps food safe without working harder than it needs to. A freezer at about minus 18 degrees is the usual recommendation. Colder than that mostly buys extra electricity use, not extra safety.
If your fridge has no temperature display, an inexpensive fridge thermometer removes the guesswork. Check it after a day, adjust the dial a little, and check again rather than making big swings.

body.heading: Seals, space and warm food
paragraphs: Door seals do quiet, important work. Clean them occasionally and test them by closing the door on a banknote: if it slides out easily, the seal may be worn and cold air could be leaking.

Let hot food cool before refrigerating it, so the fridge does not have to remove all that heat. At the same time, a reasonably full freezer runs more steadily than an empty one, because the frozen food itself holds the cold.

body.heading: Placement and patience
paragraphs: A fridge squeezed against an oven or sitting in direct sun works harder than one with air space around it. When you next move things around the kitchen, a few centimetres of breathing room behind the appliance helps it shed heat.

Try to decide what you need before opening the door, especially for children raiding snacks. Every long, thoughtful stare into the fridge is paid for twice: once in cold air lost, and once in the energy to chill the replacement air.

takeaway: Keep temperatures sensible, seals clean and doors closed, and the hardest-working appliance in the house will cost less to run.
